sections.text: This checkpoint practises Unit 1: constants, let and mut, shadowing and printing with println!. A fruit stall sells fruit by the kilo. You will write three functions: one turns text into a number and two work out prices. The main function prints the results.

It draws on the lessons Printing with println!, Variables and mutability and Shadowing. Read main as well. It uses print! to start a line that finishes with println!, and it prints a group of numbers with {:?}.

Function syntax in one line: fn name(parameter: type) -> type { ... }. The last expression, written without a semicolon, is the value the function gives back. The types of the parameters and of the result are always written out.

todo!() is a placeholder. If the program reaches it, it stops with the message "not yet implemented". Replace each todo!() with your own code. Until you do, the compiler may warn that some names are unused. That is expected.
The three constants are written outside any function, so every function can use them by name. A constant always has a written type.
In parse_kilos, &str is the type of text written in double quotes, such as "3.5". Type &str exactly like this; Unit 3 explains the &.

Hint for parse_kilos: use the shadowing pattern from the Shadowing lesson. Write let text: f64 = text.parse().unwrap(); so the new text is a number, then give it back as the last line. parse() works out which kind of number to make from the : f64.
Hint for fruit_cost: make total with let mut, multiply kilos by PRICE_PER_KILO, then add BAG_FEE with +=. The last line is total.
Hint for after_coupon: write let cost = cost - COUPON; and then another let cost line that halves it. Each new cost shadows the one before, so no mut is needed. The last line gives back cost.

exercise.prompt:
Replace each todo!() with working code. Do not change the constants or main. Inputs are never negative.

fn parse_kilos(text: &str) -> f64
Turns text such as "3.5" into an f64. The text is always a valid number. Shadow text with a new let that has the type f64, and use parse().unwrap().

fn fruit_cost(kilos: f64) -> f64
Multiplies kilos by PRICE_PER_KILO, then adds BAG_FEE. Make the total with let mut and change it with +=.

fn after_coupon(cost: f64) -> f64
Takes COUPON off cost, then halves the result. Do not use mut. Shadow cost with new let lines instead.

When the functions work, main prints:
3.5 kg costs 9.25
0 kg costs 0.5
Cost 10.5, after coupon 4.25
Cost 3, after coupon 0.5
Costs: [4.25, 5.5]

tests.label: 0 kg costs just the bag fee, 0.5
A cost of 10.5 becomes 4.25 after the coupon
A cost of 3 becomes 0.5 after the coupon
Other texts, whole numbers and fractions
Other weights use the price and then the fee
A cost equal to the coupon leaves nothing
The coupon comes off before the halving
Parsed text works with the cost function

hints: Use the constants by name inside the functions. Two functions need shadowing: parse_kilos gives text a new type, and after_coupon makes new cost variables instead of changing one. fruit_cost changes a total step by step.

In parse_kilos, shadow text with a new let of type f64, and call parse() on the old text. Add unwrap(), because parse can fail. In after_coupon, use one let cost line to take off COUPON and one to halve it.
Write let text: f64 = text.parse().unwrap(); and then text on the last line. In after_coupon, write let cost = cost - COUPON; then let cost = cost / 2.0; then cost on the last line.

quiz.question: You run cargo new fruit. Where do you write the program's code?
Which of these can give a name a new type, for example from text to a number?
What is true about a constant such as PRICE_PER_KILO?
options: It always needs a written type
It must be declared inside main
It can be changed with mut
